extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, or practitioners interested in British humour and its characteristics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the recurring themes, stylistic devices, archetypes, and historical examples that characterise British humour as presented on the Wikipedia page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong element of satire aimed at the absurdity of everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: British humour carries a strong element of satire aimed at the absurdity of everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overarching orientation appears throughout the article and underpins many subgenres; satire often targets institutions, authority and social norms (see 'Satire' section with examples such as Beyond the Fringe, That Was the Week That Was, Yes Minister, Spitting Image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common stylistic elements: sarcasm, tongue-in-cheek, banter, insults, self-deprecation, taboo subjects, puns, innuendo, wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Common themes include sarcasm, tongue-in-cheek, banter, insults, self-deprecation, taboo subjects, puns, innuendo, wit (and the British class system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are frequently combined; they appear in multiple eras and media (radio, TV, film, postcards). Use of taboo subjects and insults can be effective but risks being seen as insensitive if not subtle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A deadpan delivery is present throughout the British sense of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadpan can bury emotions and may come across as unkind to other cultures; it's a characteristic delivery mode for many British comedians and shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innuendo and double entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: Innuendo is prevalent historically (Beowulf, Chaucer) and in modern British comedy, often using double entendre and sexual suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Restoration comedy, Punch cartoons, saucy seaside postcards (Donald McGill), music-hall acts, Round the Horne, Carry On films, The Two Ronnies, Benny Hill, Monty Python's 'Nudge Nudge'. By late 20th century there was a shift toward more subtle sexual humour (Not the Nine O'Clock News, Blackadder). Contemporary examples include Julian Clary and innuendo in The Great British Bake Off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire (disrespect to establishment and authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disrespect to members of the establishment and authority is a common satirical target in British humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative works: Beyond the Fringe, That Was the Week That Was, Private Eye, Not the Nine O'Clock News, Yes Minister, Spitting Image, The Thick of It, Have I Got News for You, Brass Eye. Satire often lampoons politicians, institutions and the powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity and surrealism
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd and surreal humour—non-sequiturs, bizarre premises and sketches without conclusions—are a central strand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key examples: The Goon Show, Monty Python (sketches without conclusions), Spike Milligan's Q, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, The Mighty Boosh, Big Train, The League of Gentlemen. Often performed in a deadpan or matter-of-fact style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black humour / macabre
rubrics_metrics.description: Black humour treats topics usually regarded as serious in a humorous or satirical manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Nighty Night, Jam, Garth Marenghi's Darkplace, Murder Most Horrid, Snuff Box, Death at a Funeral, Kind Hearts and Coronets, Four Lions, Inside No. 9. This can unsettle audiences and often relies on transgressing norms about what is acceptable to joke about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal and chaotic comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaotic, anarchic, and highly physical surreal humour forms a recognized strand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bottom (violent slapstick), The Young Ones (violent slapstick, non-sequitur plots), Vic Reeves Big Night Out, other shows mixing parody of older formats with modern absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour inherent in everyday life / observational humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy that finds humour in mundane, everyday situations, often with participants unaware of the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows: Gavin & Stacey, The Office, The Royle Family, Only Fools and Horses, The Vicar of Dibley, The IT Crowd, Peep Show. Often relies on character-driven awkwardness and small social details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement and irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Understatement and irony are recurring rhetorical devices within British humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices feature across genres (see 'See also' references); understatement often functions as a comedic contrast to dramatic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word play and puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Word play, puns and linguistic cleverness are used frequently as a source of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and modern use includes Punch cartoons, The Two Ronnies, and many variety and sketch formats; double meanings (see innuendo) are a specific form of this device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adults and children / child-versus-adult conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A strand of humour focuses on tensions between children and adults (parents/teachers) and childhood mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Just William, The Beano, The Dandy, Molesworth, St Trinian's, Kevin and Perry sketches. This often frames adults as exasperated or outwitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: British class system as a comedic theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between social classes, caricaturing pompous or dim-witted upper/middle classes and social climbers, is a major theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: P. G. Wodehouse's Jeeves and Wooster, Fawlty Towers, Keeping Up Appearances, Blackadder, Dad's Army, The New Statesman. Also shows about working-class life (The Royle Family, Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lovable rogue archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: An archetype of the lovable rogue—often from the working class—trying to 'beat the system' recurs in British comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Arthur Daley (Minder), Del Trotter (Only Fools and Horses), characters in Steptoe and Son, Porridge, Rising Damp. The rogue is often resourceful, morally ambiguous, and sympathetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment of social ineptitude / awkwardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour derived from social ineptitude and embarrassment is a common device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. Bean (physical awkwardness), The Office (Ricky Gervais — cringe/awkward social interactions), Alan Partridge, Some Mothers Do 'Ave 'Em. Often uses silence, timing and character reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race and regional stereotypes (use and critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of national and regional stereotypes and accents for quick characterisation; historically included racist material which is now often rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'An Englishman, an Irishman and a Scotsman' jokes, use of regional accents in Hancock's Half Hour, Red Dwarf, Auf Wiedersehen, Pet; shows like Goodness Gracious Me subvert stereotypes. Material that relies on overt racism (e.g., certain 1970s series, comedians like Bernard Manning) is now viewed as unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bullying and harsh sarcasm (with bully coming off worse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh sarcasm and bullying feature in many works, typically with the bully ultimately losing face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: On the Buses, Blackadder (Edmund Blackadder vs Baldrick), The Young Ones, Fawlty Towers (Basil vs Manuel), The Thick of It, Bottom, The Ricky Gervais Show. This dynamic often undercuts authority or pomposity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodies of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodying British stereotypes (and others) is a common comedic tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Beyond the Fringe, Little Britain, The Fast Show, The Young Ones, Monty Python. Parody can both reinforce and critique stereotype-based humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of, and affection for, the eccentric
rubrics_metrics.description: Affection for eccentric, inventive characters and situations that celebrate oddity is a recurrent theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Heath Robinson cartoons, Wallace and Gromit, Professor Branestawm, The Vicar of Dibley, Last of the Summer Wine, A Bit of Fry and Laurie. Eccentricity is often linked to creativity and humane qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pranks and practical jokes (hidden-camera format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pranks and practical jokes—often filmed covertly—constitute a recognizable television subgenre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for TV: Candid Camera, Beadle's About, Game for a Laugh, Trigger Happy TV, Balls of Steel, Prank Patrol. These rely on unsuspecting subjects and surprise for humour.
